Holomorphic functions and conformal maps ​

Before this page

Only the calculus of functions of two real variables. The page supports Complex potentials of plane elasticity and Holes given by a conformal map.

A point of the plane, of coordinates , is the complex number    , of conjugate    . The plane problems of elasticity are solved with the functions of that have a derivative in the complex sense and with the maps they define. This appendix gives the part of their theory that those solutions use, with a proof when it is short and the reference otherwise.

1. Derivatives with respect to and ​

A function with complex values is differentiated along the two operators

They act as if and were independent variables:    and   ; the rules of the product and of the chain hold; the conjugation exchanges them,  . Their product is a quarter of the Laplacian:

For an increment    , with    and   ,

Holomorphic functions. The ratio    has a limit that does not depend on the direction of if and only if the coefficient of vanishes. A function is holomorphic in a domain when, at every point of it,

With    , the real and imaginary parts of   are the Cauchy–Riemann equations

Polynomials of , the exponential, away from the origin and their sums, products and compositions are holomorphic; is not. The conjugate of a holomorphic function, , is a function of alone:    and  .

The Jacobian matrix of   for    satisfies the two equations, its first column is , and the Laplacian of vanishes:

julia
using ForwardDiff

h(z) = exp(z) + 1 / z                             # holomorphic away from the origin
X(x) = (w = h(complex(x[1], x[2])); [real(w), imag(w)])
x = [0.7, -0.4]
J = ForwardDiff.jacobian(X, x)                    # ∂(P, Q)/∂(x₁, x₂)
HP = ForwardDiff.hessian(x -> X(x)[1], x)
z₀ = complex(x[1], x[2])
(J[1, 1] - J[2, 2], J[1, 2] + J[2, 1], complex(J[1, 1], J[2, 1]) - (exp(z₀) - 1 / z₀^2), HP[1, 1] + HP[2, 2])
(-6.661338147750939e-16, 0.0, -4.440892098500626e-16 + 0.0im, 1.3322676295501878e-15)

2. Harmonic functions ​

The real and the imaginary parts of a holomorphic function are harmonic:    , and the Laplacian is a real operator, so that   . The two are called conjugate: each determines the other, up to a constant, through the Cauchy–Riemann equations.

Conversely, on a simply connected domain, every real harmonic function is the real part of a holomorphic function. The function    is holomorphic, since   . On a simply connected domain a holomorphic function has a primitive ,   (Cauchy's theorem). Then     ; the function   is real, so that its derivative with respect to , the conjugate of the former, vanishes too: it is a constant, which is added to . On a domain with a hole the primitive may take another value after one turn around it (section 5).

3. Biharmonic functions ​

The stress function of plane elasticity satisfies   (Complex potentials of plane elasticity). On a simply connected domain, every real biharmonic function is

with and holomorphic: the form of Goursat (Muskhelishvili, section 31, equation (31.2)). It follows from     by integrating twice.

  • Let    , real. It is harmonic, so that   is holomorphic (section 2); let be a function whose second derivative is  . Then   is real and its derivative with respect to vanishes: it is a constant, added to by a term proportional to in . Thus  .

  • The function       has     . The difference    is therefore harmonic, the real part of a holomorphic (section 2).

Conversely every such is biharmonic, since   is harmonic. The check, with symbols, on for the Cauchy–Riemann equations and on  ,   for the form of Goursat:

julia
import Symbolics

Symbolics.@variables x₁ x₂
z = x₁ + im * x₂
D₁, D₂ = Symbolics.Differential(x₁), Symbolics.Differential(x₂)
∂(D, F) = Symbolics.expand_derivatives(D(F))
Δ(F) = ∂(D₁, ∂(D₁, F)) + ∂(D₂, ∂(D₂, F))
cube = z * z * z
P, Q = real(cube), imag(cube)
Symbolics.simplify.((∂(D₁, P) - ∂(D₂, Q), ∂(D₂, P) + ∂(D₁, Q), Δ(P)); expand = true)
(0, 0, 0)
julia
φ, χ = z * z, z * z * z * z
F = real(conj(z) * φ + χ)
Symbolics.simplify.((Δ(Δ(F)), Δ(F) - 4real(2z)); expand = true)   # ΔΔF and ΔF - 4 Re φ′
(0, 0)

4. Series, and their coefficients on the unit circle ​

The domains of this documentation are the outside of a hole, mapped on the outside of the unit disk (section 6). A function holomorphic for   is the sum of its Laurent series

If is bounded by at infinity,    for every large : the coefficients of the positive powers vanish, and   , with  . If grows as   at most, one positive power remains,  .

Identification on the circle. On the unit circle   , so that   and the conjugate of a series is again a series of powers of :

Since    , a series   that vanishes for every has all its coefficients zero. A boundary condition on the contour of a hole mixes a function and the conjugate of another; written on the circle, it becomes a relation between series of and is solved power by power. When the map of the hole has a finite number of terms, the sums are finite (Holes given by a conformal map, section 3, and the elliptic hole of Complex potentials of plane elasticity).

Cauchy's formula. The general tool for the same task is the Cauchy integral. For holomorphic for  , continuous up to the circle and bounded at infinity, the circle being run counterclockwise (Muskhelishvili, section 70, equations (70.1′) and (70.2′)),

The integral, computed by the trapezoidal rule on the circle, for a function with a pole inside the disk:

julia
g(ζ) = 2 + 1 / (ζ - 0.4im) + 0.3 / ζ^2            # holomorphic outside the circle, g(∞) = 2
n = 64
σs = cis.(2π * (0:(n - 1)) / n)
cauchy(ζ) = sum(g(σ) * σ / (σ - ζ) for σ in σs) / n   # dσ = i σ dθ
ζₒ, ζᵢ = 1.6 * cis(0.4), 0.5 * cis(-1.0)
abs(cauchy(ζₒ) - (2 - g(ζₒ))), abs(cauchy(ζᵢ) - 2)
(2.375126975491339e-13, 4.569276124658356e-16)

5. The logarithm, and potentials that are not single-valued ​

The function    is holomorphic in the plane without the origin, of derivative , but it is not single-valued: after one counterclockwise turn around the origin its value has increased by . Outside a hole, let be holomorphic and single-valued, of Laurent coefficients . Integrating term by term,

and is single-valued if and only if  , that is   . The potentials of plane elasticity outside a hole have such a term, proportional to the resultant of the forces applied to the hole, and it vanishes for a free hole (Complex potentials of plane elasticity, section 3).

6. Conformal maps ​

Let   be holomorphic and one-to-one on a domain, with  . Near a point,   : every small segment is turned by and stretched by , the same for all directions. Two curves keep the angle at which they cross, and a small figure keeps its shape: the map is conformal (Muskhelishvili, section 47).

The outside of a hole is the image of the outside of the unit disk by

which keeps the point at infinity at infinity; the condition that makes it one-to-one, and the shapes it gives, are in Holes given by a conformal map, section 2.

Curvilinear coordinates. With   , the images of the circles   and of the rays   cover the outside of the hole, the contour being   (Muskhelishvili, section 49, equation (49.1)). Their tangents are

the two families cross at right angles, and the ratio of the lengths is . The unit vector of increasing is the complex number and is  , with

so that a vector of components has, in the frame , the components       (Muskhelishvili's equations (49.3) and (49.4)). The contour,  , has for tangent and for normal, pointing away from the hole.

The ellipse. The map     with    gives

(Muskhelishvili's section 48, equations (48.16) to (48.18)). The circle becomes the ellipse of semi-axes  , whose foci, at , do not depend on ; eliminating , the ray becomes the branch of the hyperbola

of the same foci. The contour is the ellipse of semi-axes   along and   along . A complex coefficient    turns it by , since     with  . For   the ellipse flattens into the segment  , at whose ends vanishes.

The tangents of the image grid at a point, computed by automatic differentiation of  , are orthogonal, in the ratio , and the first one is along ; the images of a ray lie on the hyperbola:

julia
m = 0.35
ω(ζ) = ζ + m / ζ
dω(ζ) = 1 - m / ζ^2
Z(q) = (w = ω(q[1] * cis(q[2])); [real(w), imag(w)])   # (ρ, θ) ↦ (x₁, x₂)
ρ, θ = 1.4, 0.6
J = ForwardDiff.jacobian(Z, [ρ, θ])
∂ρ, ∂θ = J[:, 1], J[:, 2]
ζ = ρ * cis(θ)
eα = ζ * dω(ζ) / (ρ * abs(dω(ζ)))
(sum(∂ρ .* ∂θ), hypot(∂θ...) / hypot(∂ρ...) - ρ, abs(complex(∂ρ...) / hypot(∂ρ...) - eα))
(-1.1102230246251565e-16, 0.0, 1.5700924586837752e-16)
julia
[real(w)^2 / (4m * cos(θ)^2) - imag(w)^2 / (4m * sin(θ)^2) for w in ω.((1.0, 1.5, 2.5) .* cis(θ))]
3-element Vector{Float64}:

Where to go next ​

Complex potentials of plane elasticity writes every solution of plane elasticity with two holomorphic functions, solves the elliptic hole with the identification of section 4, and extends the method to an anisotropic matrix. Holes given by a conformal map applies it to a map of any number of terms, and Conformal holes gives the syntax; the cells of the plane in which these holes are placed are described in Problems of the plane.
